title: If you feel no shame
hookLine: among the words of earlier prophecy: if you feel no shame, do as you wish (Nawawi 20, Abu Mas'ud)
tomorrow: a man wants one sentence he'll never need to ask about again. what?

cards: A comment section at its worst has one thing in common: nobody posting seems embarrassed. Screenshots, pile-ons, a stranger's worst moment shared for a laugh. Al-Nawawi's twentieth hadith has a line for that.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it's among the words people have kept from earlier prophecy: if you feel no shame, do as you wish. So that's the line from earlier prophets.
By the hadith's own account, it's older than the hadith. Handed down.

teach.b: One question today: what keeps a person decent when nobody's checking?
This hadith, from Sahih al-Bukhari, told by Abu Mas'ud, answers with haya: shame, modesty, the inner flinch before something low. 'Do as you wish' isn't permission.
Read it as a warning, or as a description: once the flinch is gone, nothing inside is left to stop you. Not a law, not a fine, not a person watching: just the flinch, and it's gone.
Another hadith calls haya a branch of faith. Shame guards. Now the thread to a neighbor.
The hadith itself says the saying came from prophets before.

The book of Jeremiah, read by Jews and Christians, grieves over a people who lost that same flinch: "Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush."
Same alarm: the trouble isn't one wrong; it's a face that no longer blushes.
And one honest difference. Jeremiah is a prophet grieving over his own people in his own time, a lament with a name and a place.
The hadith carries the saying without naming which prophet first said it, and makes it a short rule anyone can pack.
Two traditions, guarding the same door, ranked by no one. And haya isn't self-hatred. It's the guard at the door, not a prison.

how: Muslims speak of haya as part of faith, in dress, speech and online life, and parents and teachers often quote 'if you feel no shame, do as you wish' as a gentle warning.

games.q: what does “if you feel no shame” mean?
o: a rule that shame is always unhealthy
permission to do anything you like
a warning: without shame, nothing stops you

games.q: the flinch and the neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: where the hadith says it comes from
grieves a people who can't blush

s: 'do as you wish' in the hadith is permission
it's a warning: once the flinch is gone, nothing inside stops you.
the hadith says this saying comes from earlier prophecy
Islam's own text names it as older than the hadith.
it's the guard at the door, not a prison; another hadith calls it a branch of faith.

games.q: a classmate's embarrassing video is going around. it's funny, and sharing it costs you nothing. what does today's line say about that moment?
o: the flinch is the guard; if it stops you, it's working.
shame is unhealthy; share it and don't overthink it.
share it in the small chat only, where it doesn't count.
games.why: 'if you feel no shame, do as you wish' is a warning: the flinch is what stops the share.

practice: Pick up your phone and open the last thing you posted, sent, or almost sent. Look at it as if someone you deeply respect were reading over your shoulder.
Don't delete anything; just notice whether there's a flinch, and where it sits. If there isn't one, that's fine too; you've just checked the lock.

wordCard.voice: If you feel no shame: a warning the hadith says came from earlier prophecy. Haya is the flinch that keeps you, even when no one is watching.

orig.note: Arabic: modesty, shame, a sense of honor; the guard in today's hadith.

carryVoice: Your line: shame guards. A blush isn't a failure; it's a lock that still works, on a door worth keeping. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 20; Sahih al-Bukhari 3483 (Abu Mas'ud)
Sahih al-Bukhari 9 (haya is a branch of faith)
